Higher refining margins, stronger crude prices and record US refinery throughput supported results, while the company expanded its position in Venezuela and set production records at several assets. For readers who follow Oil and Gas Stocks, Chevron is one of the most important integrated energy companies in the world. It is a major component of the energy sector on the NYSE Composite. Net income increased dramatically compared with the same quarter last year, and revenue rose at a strong double-digit pace. Adjusted earnings also topped analyst expectations, and adjusted free cash flow was very strong, helped by a loan repayment from its Kazakhstan joint venture and asset sale proceeds. Chevron's US refineries processed a record amount of crude oil during the quarter, running at very high utilization. Stronger margins on refined products such as diesel and gasoline lifted downstream earnings. The Pascagoula refinery achieved a diesel production record. Global supply disruptions linked to conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have pushed fuel prices higher, supporting refining margins across the industry. Total production declined slightly from a year earlier, mainly because higher prices reduced entitlement volumes under certain contracts and because of disruptions tied to the Middle East conflict. However, Chevron set production records at its operated assets in Australia, achieved record deepwater output in the US Gulf of America and kept Permian Basin production at a high level. US upstream production exceeded a key milestone for another consecutive quarter, and natural gas production reached a quarterly record led by Australia and the Eastern Mediterranean. Chevron has operated in Venezuela for generations. It recently secured improved commercial terms and expanded acreage there, and its joint ventures plan to invest heavily over the next several years. Following an accounting change, Chevron now includes Venezuela production in its results, and the quarter included one month of that output. Management sees the opportunity to more than double production in Venezuela over the next several years, supported by low-cost, long-duration resources. Chevron's acquisition of Hess last year added a stake in Guyana's prolific offshore oil fields and expanded its position in the Bakken region of North Dakota. These assets provide long-term production growth and help diversify Chevron's portfolio. Capital spending was lower than a year earlier, mainly because of reduced investment in the Permian Basin. Chevron expects to finish the year at the low end of its annual spending range, even though fourth-quarter spending will rise. Disciplined spending supports free cash flow and investor returns. The board declared a quarterly dividend, continuing Chevron's long record of steady payouts. Strong free cash flow supports both dividends and share repurchases. Chevron is advancing growth options in Angola, Iraq and other regions. It also expects to complete a transaction in the fourth quarter that will result in a one-time, non-cash accounting loss, which will be treated as a special item. Refining turns crude oil into fuels such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. When fuel prices rise faster than crude costs, refiners earn wider margins. For integrated companies like Chevron, strong refining results can offset weaker upstream earnings when oil prices fall, helping stabilize cash flow across the commodity cycle. This quarter, both upstream prices and refining margins supported results. The Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico is one of Chevron's most important production regions. Output there has remained at a high level for several consecutive quarters, even as the company reduced capital spending in the basin. This reflects efficiency gains from technology and longer, more productive wells, allowing Chevron to maintain output while spending less. Risks include oil and gas price volatility, refining margin normalization, Middle East supply disruptions, political risks in Venezuela, project execution and regulatory changes. Chevron and its largest US rival both benefit from integrated operations that balance upstream and downstream results. Chevron's strengths include its Permian and Australian assets, its Hess-acquired stake in Guyana and its new expansion in Venezuela, which offers a distinctive long-term growth path. Chevron owns a major interest in Tengizchevroil, a large oil project in Kazakhstan. Operations there have been running near full rates in recent months, and the venture repaid a loan to Chevron during the quarter, boosting cash flow. As this project reaches full production, it is expected to provide steady cash distributions for years. Key indicators include refining margins, Venezuela production growth, Permian and Guyana output, capital spending discipline and next year's guidance. Chevron's third quarter showed strong earnings driven by record refining performance and higher prices, while new production records and an expanding Venezuela position point to future growth. title: How Has Chevron’s Story Changed For Shareholders? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Chevron (CVX) stock trades at 15.7 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. Shareholders paying that price need to know what they are buying. Chevron’s priorities have changed. Management talked up the merger with Hess as recently as its fiscal Q2 2026 call, and emphasized other things on the fiscal Q3 2026 call. So what has taken the place of the Hess deal? Management made the case for two growth plans on the October 30, 2026 call. Chevron plans to double production at its three joint ventures in Venezuela to roughly 600,000 barrels a day by 2031, and it is increasing exploration spending by 50% relative to 2025. Across its fiscal 2025 calls, management emphasized Hess instead. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2025 call that it had closed the merger, and on the fiscal Q3 2025 call that the Hess integration was on track and synergies were being realized. The deal mattered because, in management’s words on the fiscal Q4 2025 call, it created a premier upstream portfolio with the highest cash margins in the industry. Management’s last word on Hess was good news. Chevron was capturing 50% more synergies, the savings from combining the two companies, than it first targeted, management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call. With the deal ahead of plan, management may simply have less left to say about Hess. That reads as a reason for the quieter airtime rather than a warning. Venezuela is still small next to the upstream business Hess joined. Management expects the three ventures to reach around 300,000 barrels a day of gross production by year-end, while Chevron as a whole produced nearly 4 million barrels a day in fiscal Q3 2026. That total already includes one month of production from the Venezuelan ventures. Venezuelan output is growing quickly, up 20% over the last 12 months. The upstream side of Chevron is a big business on its own. Its Upstream segment brought in $88.4 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025. That equaled 47.9% of company revenue that year, and that revenue grew 0.7% from fiscal 2024. On management’s figures, Venezuela’s growth comes cheap. Management puts total cost in Venezuela, capital and operating spending together, at less than $20 a barrel, and it expects no major additional infrastructure spending as production doubles. Management also says the program will pay for itself. The doubling, though, is a plan that runs to 2031, not a result. So far, yes, but Chevron’s low P/E comes from profit that has swung widely. Chevron earned $27.0 billion over the last twelve months, up from $12.8 billion in the twelve months before. Quarterly profit moved from $2.21 billion in fiscal Q1 2026 to $12.1 billion in fiscal Q2. Management said oil prices moved across a $64 range within the third quarter alone. That is why the Hess fields still matter to what you own. The Hess assets generate free cash flow roughly double the extra dividends the deal added, management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call. If those fields slip, part of the cash behind Chevron’s 3.3% dividend yield goes with them. If Venezuela costs more than management expects, the main source of the production growth it now talks up would weaken. Management has reported Hess synergies ahead of target, while the Venezuela growth it now emphasizes is still a plan. When Chevron reports in January 2027, production from the Venezuelan ventures against management’s year-end goal is the number to watch. With ImmunityBio (IBRX) shares up more than 200% this year, founder Patrick Soon-Shiong has outlined plans to unveil decades of privately funded research at NantWorks over the next 12 months, spanning cancer therapies, AI chips and satellite tech. IBRX stock tumbled 9% on Thursday to $6.07, with shares down 30% for the week and tracking their worst week in nearly two years. Soon-Shiong said on X: “I began the release of our stealth, self-funded programs at Nantworks at a speech at Stanford last night.” NantWorks brings together public and private businesses across healthcare, energy and communications. Soon-Shiong highlighted an antibody search engine he likened to Google, part of an effort to find and treat tumors more precisely. He said that the search engine will use camelid antibodies to make tumors visible on PET scans, then targeting them with radioactive isotopes. The goal is to connect cancer detection with treatment directed at the tumor. He also outlined a system that gives doctors real-time patient data to help them make timely treatment decisions. Soon-Shiong said the tech already had FDA approval, but did not name the product. Meanwhile, Soon-Shiong outlined tech to move data faster as AI systems grow. These include high-speed WiGig wireless tech and optical chips that transmit data using light. He also highlighted U.S. factories to make optical chips and chipsets that connect AI data centers. NantOptiFab is already working in this area, making chips in California that use light to carry information for AI networks, space systems and quantum technology. An SEC filing in August named Soon-Shiong as a director and showed that the company raised $20 million by selling shares to one unnamed investor. His space ambitions include chips for use in space, satellite terminals that communicate using light, and new ways to build and launch satellites. The projects also extend to energy, materials and food safety. Soon-Shiong listed batteries that work in Arctic conditions, non-toxic methods of making graphene, biodegradable alternatives to plastic made from ocean-derived materials, and machine vision to detect harmful substances in food and baby food at the point of purchase. Soon-Shiong also spotlighted a blockchain-based exchange for tokenized securities, or digital versions of stocks and other investments. He pitched it as a way to give companies and investors more control. In January, Nant Global Finance announced plans to bring stock trading, shareholder records and blockchain settlement onto one platform. Its acquisitions included Horizon Globex, which provides technology for the Upstream exchange, and BlockAgent and Equity Stock Transfer, which maintain shareholder records. The company also planned to rename Arkonis Capital, a brokerage and trading platform, NantX. At the time, completing its brokerage acquisitions still required approval from the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA). Soon-Shiong also circled back to ImmunityBio’s work on IL-15, a protein that helps activate the body’s immune defenses. Its drug Anktiva stimulates natural killer cells and T cells, which fight cancer and infections. The company is testing whether it can help patients whose immune-cell counts are too low, a condition called lymphopenia. This also includes a sepsis trial that Soon-Shiong said had been authorized. “Trials will be starting soon in USA and Europe,” he said on Wednesday. The Phase 2 study will test Anktiva in about 50 critically ill adults with sepsis and low immune-cell counts. Researchers will compare the drug plus standard care with standard care alone to see whether it reduces deaths within 28 days. “Longevity at work. Book of our patients’ stories soon,” Soon-Shiong said. The drug is already approved in the U.S. with BCG for certain bladder cancers. ImmunityBio’s approval last month expanded its use to another group of patients whose cancer had not responded to BCG. The update comes shortly after ImmunityBio’s third-quarter results, which showed that net product revenue rose 53% from a year earlier to $48.7 million. For the first nine months, it grew 92% to $143.6 million. The company also said its Quilt-2.005 trial met its main goal in a group of bladder cancer patients who had not previously received BCG. The company is on track to seek expanded FDA approval for these patients in the fourth quarter. Shares of Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) surged 17% in after-hours trading on Thursday after the company said that its key leukemia trial results are expected this month, with its CEO pointing to the treatment’s potential to become a “transformative” immunotherapy if successful. SLS stock fell nearly 5% on Thursday to $8.03, with shares on track to post their third straight weekly decline. The update is related to the Phase 3 Regal trial of Galinpepimut-S (GPS) in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The November timeline narrows Sellas’ earlier guidance for results in the fourth quarter. “In our ongoing Phase 3 REGAL trial of GPS, we are focused on completing the final analysis following the announcement of 80th event, and we expect to announce topline primary endpoint results this month,” CEO Angelos Stergiou said. “If successful, we believe GPS could be a transformative new immunotherapy for AML patients in second complete remission.” Regal is testing GPS as a maintenance treatment for AML patients who have returned to remission after treatment for a relapse. The study’s main goal is to determine whether GPS helps these patients live longer. GPS is licensed from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and targets WT1, a protein found in a range of cancers. Sellas disclosed late last month that the trial had reached its prespecified 80th death, the milestone required to begin its final analysis. This process involves finalizing and reviewing the trial database, revealing treatment assignments and analyzing the results. Beyond GPS, Sellas is advancing its second leukemia drug, Tambiciclib, or SLS009, with investors looking ahead to fresh trial results and a major medical conference presentation. The company has enrolled 40 patients in its planned 80-patient Phase 2 study in newly diagnosed AML, up from 28 disclosed in August. The study includes patients whose disease stops responding early to Azacitidine and Venetoclax, an existing drug combination. Enrollment and treatment are currently continuing, with preliminary results expected in the fourth quarter. The development comes after a completed Phase 2 study in patients whose leukemia returned or failed to respond after prior Venetoclax-based treatment. Sellas will present the findings on Dec.14 at the American Society of Hematology (ASH) meeting in New Orleans. The study enrolled 62 patients and combined SLS009 with azacitidine and venetoclax. Across all doses, 34% of the 59 patients evaluated responded to treatment. At the dose of 30 milligrams twice weekly, 54% of patients with monocytic AML, a leukemia subtype, responded, with median survival of 5.8 months. Among patients with a TP53 mutation, 57% responded, with median survival of 8.8 months. Sellas ended September with $134.7 million in cash and cash equivalents, down from $138.3 million in June. “With $134.7 million in cash and cash equivalents as of September 30, we are well positioned to further advance these programs,” Stergiou said. Third-quarter (Q3) net loss widened to $10.1 million from $6.8 million a year earlier, while loss per share narrowed to $0.05 from $0.06. Meanwhile, research and development spending rose to $7 million from $4.2 million as Sellas prepared for a potential GPS approval application after Regal’s final analysis. Additionally, Sellas is preparing to study SLS009 in pancreatic cancer patients after laboratory findings presented in September. Working with the University of Wisconsin-Madison, researchers tested SLS009 in cancer models grown from patient tissue, including one resistant to Daraxonrasib. They also tested it alongside the experimental drug ZEN3694. Sellas said that the findings support further research into overcoming treatment resistance. However, patient trials are yet to begin. content: Chevron's Q3 adjusted profit nearly tripled to $10.4 billion, even as production fell 2.6%. Surging refining margins drove downstream earnings up 333%, with Chevron's refineries operating at 98% capacity. Chevron's integrated business model helped offset lower production, underscoring its resilience and 39-year streak of dividend increases. Since the start of the year, the conflict in Iran has resulted in disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 million barrels of oil pass daily. Oil prices have jumped. More importantly, diesel fuel and other refined products have surged. By operating across the value chain, Chevron has a natural hedge that helps it weather major fluctuations in crude oil prices and fuel and other refined products. In the third quarter, production dropped by roughly 106,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, or roughly 2.6%. This was driven in part by fewer physical barrels under production -- sharing contract entitlements and by disruptions in the Middle East. While production fell, upstream earnings surged 72% to $5.7 billion. On top of this, downstream refining margins exploded as global refining capacity took a hit amid the Iran conflict, with strikes hitting facilities in the Middle East and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries taking roughly 10% of the world's fuel-making capacity offline. As a result, Chevron's refineries operated at 98% capacity, and downstream earnings surged 333% year over year to $4.9 billion. content: Fewer barrels, bigger profits: Chevron's latest quarter highlights the strength of its integrated business model. Since the start of the year, the conflict in Iran has resulted in disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 million barrels of oil pass daily. Oil prices have jumped. More importantly, diesel fuel and other refined products have surged. Chevron's (CVX +1.64%) third-quarter adjusted profit nearly tripled year over year to $10.4 billion, despite production declining 2.6%. The seemingly contradictory move illustrates the advantages of Chevron's integrated business model. Here's what investors should know. As an integrated oil and gas company, Chevron's business spans upstream exploration and production of crude oil and natural gas, as well as downstream refining and fuel sales. By operating across the value chain, Chevron has a natural hedge that helps it weather major fluctuations in crude oil prices and fuel and other refined products. In the third quarter, production dropped by roughly 106,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, or roughly 2.6%. This was driven in part by fewer physical barrels under production -- sharing contract entitlements and by disruptions in the Middle East. While production fell, upstream earnings surged 72% to $5.7 billion. On top of this, downstream refining margins exploded as global refining capacity took a hit amid the Iran conflict, with strikes hitting facilities in the Middle East and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries taking roughly 10% of the world's fuel-making capacity offline. As a result, Chevron's refineries operated at 98% capacity, and downstream earnings surged 333% year over year to $4.9 billion. Chevron is a top integrated oil and gas company vital to the energy complex, and this year illustrated the strengths of its integrated business model and capital discipline, showing why it continues to deliver for long-term investors with 39 consecutive years of dividend increases. title: Chevron Q3 Earnings Surge on Strong Refining: Is the Stock a Buy Now? - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation CVX posted a sharp increase in third-quarter 2026 earnings, as stronger refining margins and record U.S. refinery throughput helped lift profitability. The energy giant earned $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per diluted share, compared with $3.54 billion, or $1.82, a year earlier. Adjusted earnings reached $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. The strong results were accompanied by healthy cash generation, rising earnings estimates and continued shareholder returns. Chevron has also delivered better year-to-date share-price performance than integrated energy peers ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM and Shell plc SHEL. Let's examine the factors supporting its investment case. Chevron's downstream business played a major role in its third-quarter earnings growth. The segment generated $4.93 billion in earnings, up from $1.14 billion a year earlier, benefiting from stronger refining margins and reliable operations. This improvement was particularly noticeable in the United States, where downstream earnings jumped to $3.59 billion from $638 million in the year-ago quarter. U.S. refinery crude throughput reached a record 1.09 million barrels per day, with capacity utilization approaching 98%. Chevron is also making better use of its existing refining infrastructure. At the Pasadena refinery, the company increased processing capacity by approximately 15% through debottlenecking improvements, adding throughput capacity at relatively little cost. These initiatives highlight Chevron's focus on getting more value from its assets. Much like ExxonMobil and Shell, Chevron's integrated operations allow it to participate across the energy value chain, with refining serving as an important contributor to overall earnings. Analysts have become more optimistic about Chevron's earnings outlook, as reflected in upward revisions of the consensus estimates. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate trend for Chevron's 2026 earnings has risen 12.90%, while the same for 2027 has increased 22.85%. ExxonMobil's earnings estimates for 2026 and 2027 have increased 12.60% and 15.45%, respectively. Shell has recorded corresponding increases of 13.69% and 10.64%. While all three companies have seen upward revisions, Chevron stands out for 2027, with its estimate increasing more sharply than those of both peers. The stronger revisions suggest growing confidence in Chevron's ability to sustain earnings performance. Its refining operations, disciplined spending and expanding production opportunities provide several potential drivers of future profitability. Chevron's valuation also merits attention. The stock trades at 11.76 times forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E), slightly below ExxonMobil's multiple of 12.13 times. Shell, meanwhile, trades at 8.91 times. Although Chevron commands a premium over Shell, the modest discount to ExxonMobil offers an interesting comparison, particularly given its recent earnings performance and improving analyst expectations. Chevron's combination of reliable operations, substantial cash generation and shareholder distributions provides support for its valuation. For investors looking to gain exposure to a diversified energy producer, CVX offers an appealing mix of earnings potential and financial stability. Chevron has also performed well in the stock market. Shares of CVX have gained approximately 39.8% year to date, ahead of ExxonMobil's 38.4% increase and Shell's 33.2% rise. That gives Chevron a lead of 1.4 percentage points over ExxonMobil and 6.6 percentage points over Shell. The share-price gains have come alongside strong refining profitability, solid cash generation and improving earnings expectations. These developments have helped strengthen Chevron's standing among major integrated energy companies. With analysts continuing to raise their earnings estimates, Chevron has additional fundamental support for its investment outlook. Cash Flow and Expansion Plans Support Long-Term Growth Chevron's cash-generating ability remains a key attraction. The company generated $16 billion in operating cash flow during the third quarter, while adjusted free cash flow reached $14.2 billion. The company returned $6 billion to its shareholders, comprising $3.5 billion in dividends and $2.5 billion in share repurchases. Chevron also reduced total debt by approximately $3.5 billion during the quarter, further strengthening its balance sheet. Its production operations continue to deliver encouraging results. U.S. output exceeded 2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day for the fifth consecutive quarter. Production in the Permian Basin remained around 1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day for the sixth straight quarter. Chevron is also positioning itself for future expansion. Its Venezuelan joint ventures are targeting approximately 600,000 barrels per day of gross production by 2031, creating another potential avenue for growth. Together, steady production, capital discipline and strategic investments provide a strong foundation for Chevron's longer-term prospects. Chevron's third-quarter results offer several reasons for optimism. Strong refining profitability, record U.S. crude throughput and substantial cash generation demonstrate the company's ability to make the most of its integrated operations. Rising earnings estimates, a competitive valuation relative to ExxonMobil and better year-to-date share-price performance than both XOM and SHEL further strengthen the investment case. Chevron's commitment to shareholder returns and its plans to expand production add to the positives. With a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), CVX looks attractive for investors seeking exposure to the integrated energy industry. Its combination of solid earnings, healthy cash flow and long-term growth opportunities makes the stock worth considering for an investment portfolio. title: South Korea’s 270-Metre Drone Carrier Plan Shifts Focus From F-35Bs to Indo-Pacific Fleet Command - Defence Security Asia
content:
Defence Security Asia - Asian Defence and Security Affairs

Majalah pertahanan Asia PIA Flight PK404: India Shoot-Down Claim Resurfaces After Glacier Video Iran Claims US Early-Warning Radar Hit in Bahrain, Raising Stakes for Hormuz US Arms Philippine Marines With a New Surveillance Tool: Devil Ray T38 Drones (DEFENCE SECURITY ASIA) — South Korea’s navy has proposed a 270-metre drone carrier to succeed its stalled F-35B-centred CVX programme, betting that a fleet built around maritime surveillance and command can give Seoul greater influence over how regional crises are monitored and managed.Explore History At the October 20, 2026 parliamentary audit at Gyeryongdae, Chief of  Naval Operations Admiral Kim Kyung-ryul presented a design concept exceeding 30,000 tonnes in light displacement, more than twice that of the roughly 14,000-tonne Dokdo class. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff were still reviewing the revised requirement at the time of the audit, with a decision expected by the end of 2026 and an early-2040s service target superseding the previous late-2030s window.Explore History The Republic of Korea Navy intends to embark more than 20 unmanned systems across several categories, a measure of mission breadth that leaves open questions about aircraft availability for any single task over a deployment. The transition from an F-35B-centred air wing to manned-unmanned teaming shifts the emphasis from embarked fighter aviation to the coordination of reconnaissance aircraft, combat drones, helicopters and uncrewed surface vessels within a larger South Korean  naval force.Compare Cars Admiral Kim Kyung-ryul, the Republic of Korea’s Chief of Naval Operations, has linked naval strength to sovereignty, maritime security and prosperity, framing disruption to sea routes as an economic risk and widening the carrier debate beyond peninsula deterrence. The proposal arrives alongside plans for nuclear-powered attack submarines, KDDX destroyers and intelligence collection ships, each with an earlier target window that could make those programmes earlier measures of changes in its maritime force posture. The large angled flight deck allows for a broader aviation mix, while the absence of published launch and recovery specifications leaves the compatibility of future unmanned combat aircraft with the ship unresolved at the requirements stage. A fleet able to sustain surveillance and coordinate dispersed ships beyond the Korean Peninsula would give Seoul more options in regional crises, particularly when allied priorities diverge or maritime disruption threatens trade routes that South Korea depends on. The carrier’s logistics footprint would extend beyond aviation fuel and spare parts to the maintenance and support of several families of uncrewed systems, making the manpower and sustainment burden central to comparisons with the original fighter-carrier model. The Navy also envisages amphibious support and disaster relief, broadening the ship’s peacetime and crisis utility while introducing competing demands for deck space, embarked personnel and transport capacity for the eventual design and operating concept to reconcile. The procurement choice will test how far Seoul is prepared to extend its naval role beyond peninsula defence while committing escorts, crews and maintenance capacity to a flagship that would share resources with the submarines and destroyers already in its plans. The original CVX grew out of LPX-II under President Moon Jae-in, and its proposed complement of roughly 16 to 20 F-35Bs would have given South Korea an embarked short take-off and vertical landing fighter force alongside helicopters for supporting missions. The early CVX programme targeted service around 2033 and entailed costs ranging from ship construction to aircraft acquisition, aircrew training and through-life support for a naval aviation community that Seoul would have had to establish. The 2023 defence budget proposal allocated no funding to CVX, while South Korea prioritised additional land-based F-35As, illustrating how pressure to reinforce near-term peninsula deterrence could outweigh the case for an embarked fighter force whose benefits would arrive years later. Under President Yoon Suk-yeol, the three-axis deterrence system gained priority, sharpening the competition between CVX and investments in missile defence, conventional strike and other capabilities with more direct roles in South Korea’s response to North Korean nuclear and missile threats. The Navy outlined its drone-centred direction to lawmakers in May 2025 and submitted the revised operational requirement in October, giving manned-unmanned teaming a formal place in force planning after several years of uncertainty over the original carrier’s mission and funding. Under then-Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Kang Dong-gil, the October 2025 audit put service in the late 2030s, so the early-2040s target under Admiral Kim leaves a longer interval in which existing ships will carry the Navy’s shipborne aviation ambitions. The Navy drew on lessons from Ukraine to justify greater investment in drones and artificial intelligence, although the relevance of those lessons to sustained naval aviation depends on how well uncrewed aircraft perform across repeated cycles of sea-based operations and maintenance. Navy Sea GHOST provides the doctrinal context for the revised carrier, linking crewed ships with unmanned air, surface and underwater systems and making fleet integration a programme objective that can be pursued before the proposed flagship reaches operational service in the 2040s. Dropping the F-35B air wing removes a major prospective procurement expense and shifts part of the programme’s industrial focus toward South Korean shipbuilders, while the eventual aircraft and shipboard equipment selections will determine how much reliance on foreign suppliers changes. South Korea’s demographic pressures help explain the attraction of a more technology-intensive fleet, but a shift toward uncrewed platforms could transfer some staffing demands to aircraft maintenance, software support and mission supervision, making total personnel requirements more informative than ship’s company alone. The public outline puts the ship at 270 metres long and 70 metres wide, with light displacement above 30,000 tonnes, giving the Navy a much larger aviation platform than Dokdo while leaving full-load displacement and the final hull form unresolved. Against the roughly 250-metre by 40-metre baseline cited for an earlier concept, the revised dimensions imply a substantially wider operating envelope, although the Navy has yet to publish enough detail to determine how that width is divided between deck and hull. An angled flight deck is an explicit feature of the proposal, but the Navy has disclosed neither a catapult selection nor a recovery system, leaving no firm basis for projecting aircraft compatibility, turnaround times or the tempo of sustained fixed-wing operations. The planned unmanned complement spans combat aircraft, surveillance drones, one-way attack drones and surface vessels, so the headline capacity figure combines systems that place very different demands on deck handling, storage, maintenance and the number of operators the ship must accommodate. Reconnaissance drones could widen Seoul’s independent maritime picture, giving South Korean commanders more evidence on which to base national decisions and more information to share with partners, provided the fleet can sustain collection and assess what the aircraft report. Transport and attack helicopters would preserve an aviation role in amphibious operations, and high-speed landing craft would broaden the ship’s transport options, creating a design trade-off between accommodating several mission types and retaining sufficient space to sustain each of them. A well deck remains a possibility rather than a confirmed feature, a distinction that matters because the choice of how to handle landing craft and uncrewed surface vessels affects the ship’s internal arrangement and its balance between aviation and amphibious functions. Hanwha Ocean’s Ghost Commander II pairs a roughly 42,000-tonne concept with electromagnetic catapults and a well deck, illustrating one industry approach to mixed operations while leaving the Navy’s own launch equipment, internal layout and choice of builder open to review. HD Hyundai’s smaller HCX-23 Plus concept uses a dual-deck arrangement, illustrating how differently domestic shipbuilders have interpreted the drone-carrier mission and why comparisons of tonnage or deck area alone tell little about the final mix of aviation and amphibious capacity. The Navy has released no confirmed propulsion, speed, crew size, armament or hangar capacity, leaving the headline dimensions useful for judging ambition while the evidence for assessing endurance, personnel burden and compatibility with other fleet units remains largely unavailable. The manned-unmanned battle group envisages a networked flagship coordinating dispersed assets, an arrangement whose value depends on whether information from aircraft, surface craft and other ships can reach commanders in a form they can interpret and use across the fleet. Managing a mixed embarked force would add inventory and maintenance demands because an uncrewed aircraft, a helicopter and an uncrewed surface vessel have different servicing cycles, spare parts and specialist requirements even when all three share the same deployment and support chain. An embarked total also says little about readiness across a deployment, because aircraft undergoing inspections or repair draw on hangar space and technical staff even when they are unavailable to fly, limiting what nominal capacity reveals about persistent maritime surveillance. Communications disruption is a material constraint for any networked fleet, making resilience and clear supervision important measures of programme maturity, especially when uncrewed assets are expected to contribute information while the flagship is also managing helicopter or amphibious activity nearby. An uncrewed air wing may change the distribution of personnel between the ship and shore, with software maintenance, training and certification requirements creating support demands that are easy to overlook when programme comparisons focus mainly on the number of people embarked. The planned adaptation of Dokdo and Marado for UAV and command roles gives South Korea a nearer-term way to develop deck procedures and assess how much maintenance and operator capacity a mixed crewed and uncrewed deployment places on amphibious ships. Two developmental loitering munitions reportedly crashed shortly after launch during a 2026 trial from ROKS Marado, a result specific to those test rounds that nevertheless illustrates the gap between embarking an unmanned system and demonstrating reliable operation from a  naval platform. A flagship intended for disaster relief and amphibious support would need enough flexibility to accommodate different combinations of aircraft, craft and personnel, and the time required to reconfigure between assignments would shape the ship’s usefulness during a rapidly developing regional crisis. With the Navy also emphasising ship maintenance and civil-military cooperation, the carrier’s scale makes access to suitable repair facilities and long-term industrial support a force-planning question, since time in refit would directly reduce the availability of the proposed flagship. With only one hull described in the outline, every extended refit could interrupt the carrier’s contribution to regional deployments, making Dokdo and Marado important to the continuity of South Korean naval engagement even if they offer a different mix of capabilities. South Korea’s planned conventionally armed Jangbogo-N nuclear-powered attack submarines are intended to strengthen persistent undersea surveillance, giving the Navy a separate means of monitoring North Korean naval activity before the proposed carrier reaches the early-2040s window for its own operational debut. The submarine plan envisages at least three boats of roughly 8,000 tonnes, with the lead boat targeted for launch in the mid-2030s and service in the late 2030s, placing an ambitious domestic undersea programme ahead of the carrier in the timetable. The nuclear-powered submarine initiative also has an alliance dimension through the 2025 United States–South Korea summit agreement, while unresolved fuel-supply and cost questions leave its timetable exposed to decisions extending beyond the Navy and its preferred domestic shipbuilding arrangements. The next-generation KDDX destroyer offers a different contribution to South Korean force posture, combining a planned indigenous combat management system and phased-array radar with air-defence, surface warfare and anti-submarine roles that would remain relevant across several kinds of naval task group. With the first KDDX delivery targeted for 2032 and six ships envisaged, the destroyer programme could shape the surface fleet well before the carrier enters service, although no public plan in the audit defines a permanent escort allocation for the flagship. Plans for two new maritime intelligence ships by around 2035 would also add dedicated signals and acoustic collection capacity, giving Seoul a separate means of sustaining maritime awareness while a carrier’s surveillance contribution would depend on its embarked systems and availability. The audit placed ship-to-surface ballistic missiles and SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors within the same modernisation portfolio, indicating that Seoul’s maritime contribution to deterrence already includes strike and missile defence functions assigned to other ships independently of the carrier decision. Within South Korea’s three-axis deterrence architecture, the carrier’s clearest prospective contribution is maritime awareness and coordination, while dedicated combatants’ separately planned defensive and strike roles could reinforce peninsula deterrence years before the flagship contributes to the fleet’s posture. Different programme schedules create a risk of uneven readiness, because destroyers, intelligence ships, submarines and uncrewed aviation will require distinct training and support pipelines even where the Navy eventually expects them to contribute to a common fleet posture and strategic message. If crew, maintenance and escort demands rise across the fleet at the same time, the carrier’s regional utility will depend on whether it adds maritime coverage without drawing resources away from ships already tasked with peninsula surveillance and deterrence. The October audit signalled that Seoul still wants a large aviation ship after CVX stalled, but the emphasis on surveillance, maritime command and amphibious support points toward a regional role built around gathering information and coordinating a response at sea. For the United States and other regional partners, a South Korean fleet with greater surveillance and command capacity could broaden cooperation on maritime awareness and crisis response, provided information-sharing arrangements and decisions on deployment support that role in practice. For Pyongyang, the nearer-term change in South Korean  naval posture would come from the planned destroyers, surveillance ships and submarines, because their earlier service targets give them a clearer path to influencing peninsula deterrence before the carrier could deploy. From Beijing and Moscow, the earlier arrival of dedicated intelligence ships would be the more concrete sign of expanded South Korean maritime observation, while a later carrier deployment could make Seoul’s role in regional exercises and partner operations more visible. Exercises and disaster relief could turn that visibility into practical cooperation by familiarising partners with South Korean command procedures, although Seoul’s ability to sustain those commitments would narrow whenever a peninsula crisis draws ships and crews back toward home waters. Domestic industry has demonstrated interest through competing designs, yet integrating ship construction, aviation and digital systems carries delivery risk that neither a public exhibition model nor the Navy’s proposed hull dimensions can resolve at the current stage. The end-2026 Joint Chiefs of Staff decision anticipated at the audit is the next milestone for determining whether the revised requirement advances and could open the way to funding, design responsibility and the timetable for selecting compatible embarked systems. The revised carrier has no published programme cost, leaving any comparison with the earlier CVX dependent on future estimates that account for the ship, its embarked systems, personnel, support infrastructure and maintenance over its service life. Even after a favourable decision, milestones for aircraft selection and shipboard trials will say more about usable capability than the announced service date alone, because the force depends on the ship and its embarked systems reaching sufficient maturity at broadly compatible times. The geopolitical payoff would be a South Korea better able to assess maritime events independently and contribute to regional responses, but that influence depends on how often the fleet can deploy the flagship while sustaining its commitments on the peninsula. title: Exxon, Chevron, and Shell Just Reported. Here's What Each One Said About Where Oil Goes Next. - The Globe and Mail
content: Exxon specifically noted that the Middle East will remain a key driver of energy prices. Chevron highlighted that maintaining a strong financial position is vital during periods of highly volatile oil prices. Shell explained that energy security is an increasingly important topic, which can make price less of an issue for buyers. ExxonMobil(NYSE: XOM), Shell(NYSE: SHEL), and Chevron(NYSE: CVX) have their fingers on the pulse of the global energy market. However, energy is a commodity, so the best these integrated energy giants can do is react to what is taking place around them. Right now, with energy prices high, that's leading to strong financial results. However, the key issue is the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East. This highly uncertain event has upended global energy markets, leaving energy companies and entire countries in flux. Here's what Exxon, Shell, and Chevron were thinking about when they discussed earnings. The big picture: Be prepared for continued uncertainty. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Exxon reported strong third-quarter 2026 earnings, with GAAP earnings of $3.72 per share, up from $1.76 a year earlier. Adjusted earnings rose from $3.52 in the second quarter of 2026 to $4.23 in the third, a jump of 20% in a single quarter. That highlights just how volatile the energy sector is today. And the company is very clear about where that volatility is coming from, noting that "The pace of recovery in the Middle East and the broader market environment remain critical uncertainties." Essentially, that hints that the company's outlook is for elevated energy prices if the conflict continues and lower prices if the conflict draws to an end. That's not a unique perspective; Shell and Chevron pretty clearly believe the same thing. Notably, Chevron, another of the world's largest energy companies, is making a specific change to address the issue by reducing leverage. After an analyst on the company's earnings call highlighted the strength of Chevron's balance sheet, the company made a point of saying it wasn't looking to change its capital priorities. Chevron's debt-to-equity ratio is 0.17x, second only to Exxon's 0.13x. That said, Chevron, Shell, and Exxon have all been reducing leverage. A key reason for Chevron's financial prudence is its inability to predict oil price movements. Management noted that oil prices ranged from $68 to $132, a huge $64-per-barrel spread in just the third quarter. Given that backdrop, it makes complete sense that balance sheet strength remains important. And since geopolitical conflict and investor sentiment around it are key drivers of oil prices today, being prepared for volatility is really the best thing any company can do. That said, there's a changing dynamic in the global energy market that will likely linger long after the Middle East conflict ends. Shell, for example, has been in discussions with customers that range from companies to entire countries. And an increasingly important issue is energy security. Essentially, the conflict in the Middle East has increased the importance of having access to oil and natural gas that come from economically and politically stable regions. To that end, Shell highlighted that it recently gave the green light to a large expansion of a liquefied natural gas export facility in Canada. That investment, made along with project partners, will double the size of the export facility. While the project won't be complete until the early 2030s, that actually speaks to the long-term change Shell expects in the market. And management clearly highlighted on its conference call that energy security issues may lead customers to be less price-conscious. Unfortunately, there's really no clear way to know what happens next with oil prices. That's very clear when you examine what Exxon, Chevron, and Shell are saying. However, for investors, the bigger takeaway is that these global energy giants are preparing for continued uncertainty. Being in a state of flux isn't easy, but Exxon, Chevron, and Shell are all preparing for the immediate impact of that uncertainty and the long-term changes it may bring to the global energy market.
